dossier.summary: The paper argues that pooling data from ramp-up stages with different treatment proportions reduces the bias of regression-based GATE estimators under network interference. It gives a closed-form bias analysis for a graph-agnostic OLS estimator and GNN simulations on FB-Stanford3. The linear theory is internally consistent: the Table 10 biases match Theorems 3.5-3.6. All GNN numbers in Tables 1 and 3-9 recompute exactly from the delivered result arrays, but over 1000 repetitions, not the stated 100. The empirical support is weaker than claimed. The baselines are only the same estimator on one stage and a deliberately misspecified OLS, with no exposure-based regression baseline. Nearly everything runs on one graph and one parameter setting, and the "synergy" with cluster randomization is neither tested as an interaction nor uniform across tables. The code shows that the repeated-experiment control merges identical assignments, the "temporally independent" variant is still nested, and the dynamic-graph runs train on the final graph. Table 7 unit-level statistics include five unfinished all-zero repetitions. A possible node-order misalignment between GNN features and the DGL graph, flagged in the delivery's own migration notes, leaves open whether the GNN exploits micro-level exposures at all. Tables 2, 10-14 and the exposure variances have no delivered code or result files.

claims.quote: We present a closed-form bias–variance analysis of the linear regression estimator and show that, in practical settings, the bias term dominates.
we show that regression-based estimators trained on merged data achieve substantial bias reduction, even under simple randomization schemes and regression models.

issues.quote: Extensive simulations across challenging scenarios confirm that our methodology significantly improves the accuracy of regression-based estimators.
issues.why: Every interference model is run on one graph (FB-Stanford3; MIT8 only for 2-hop), one parameter setting (1,1,1,0.1), one ramp schedule and one untuned GNN, so the general "across challenging scenarios" claim reaches beyond what was varied; the square-root c~0 pairing (Table 6 right) even shows MSE rising from 0.020 to 0.280 as c_t grows, which goes undiscussed.

issues.quote: In this paper, we focus on two regression model classes, linear regression $\mathscr{F}_{\text{LR}}$ and graph neural networks $\mathscr{F}_{\text{GNN}}$, and develop a data-centric approach for bias reduction in regression-based estimation.
issues.why: The only regression baseline is a deliberately graph-agnostic OLS on (1, z). There is no exposure-based regression adjustment (e.g., regressing on the fraction of treated neighbours, which is unbiased under linear-in-means with a single experiment; chin2019regression sits in ref.bib but is never cited). The non-regression estimators (Hájek, MII) are run only on one 50% stage under 2-hop, and Lagrange interpolation only under multiplicative and square-root interference.

issues.quote: Merging stages with different treatment proportions reduces this bias by increasing exposure variation.
issues.why: Exposure variance is reported only for a few 1-hop configurations (Figure 2), and no experiment varies exposure variance while holding proportions, sample size and training steps fixed. The repeated-experiment control reuses the identical treated set (see code mismatches), and the code does not show that the GNN uses micro-level neighbour exposures (possible feature/graph misalignment).

issues.quote: (ii) \textbf{merging and cluster-level randomization act synergistically} by jointly enriching exposure variation
issues.why: No interaction is tested, and cluster-level is not uniformly better. Multiplicative t=3-5 cluster MSE is 0.017/0.019/0.030 vs unit 0.010/0.023/0.025; under square-root with c~0 pairs, cluster is worse in every row; and in 2-hop the relative merging gain is similar at both levels (unit 1.963->0.025, cluster 0.904->0.008).

issues.quote: our methodology significantly improves the accuracy
issues.why: "Significantly" has no test or confidence interval behind it; only the per-cell Std of the estimates is given. The main bias reductions are many Std wide, so the main claim survives.

issues.quote: Bias and standard deviation (Std) are estimated from 100 Monte Carlo repetitions.
issues.why: The delivered result arrays have 1000 rows (the notebooks set repeat_num = 1000), and the published Tables 1 and 3-9 recompute exactly only when all 1000 rows are used.

issues.quote: and we examine this for the linear regression estimator here
issues.why: Appendix B.4 says the repeated-experiment check uses the linear regression estimator, yet Table 2 is labelled 2-hop and its t=1 row (-1.402/0.034) matches the GNN 2-hop baseline of Table 1. The delivered repeated-experiment arrays are linear-in-means GNN runs that match neither.

issues.quote: Under unit-level randomization, MSE falls from $1.963$ at $t=1$ to $0.374$ at $t=2$ and $0.025$ at $t=4$, while the fifth stage leaves it at $0.026$.
issues.why: The t=4 vs t=5 differences used to argue non-monotone gains (0.025 vs 0.026 unit; 0.008 vs 0.010 cluster) are about one Monte Carlo standard error of the bias (Std 0.015-0.070 over the runs), so they do not show an effect of the fifth stage.

issues.quote: merging only the two extreme steps $c_1$ and $c_T$ is already sufficiently effective
issues.why: For the GNN in the main 2-hop table, the (c~0, 0.5) pair (MSE 0.033) is worse than merging the last four stages (0.025), and it is much worse under quadratic and square-root interference; the paper partly concedes the nonlinear cases in conclusion (iv).

issues.quote: Nonetheless, our methodology consistently enhances the GNN model's performance.
issues.why: The dynamic-graph unit-level numbers (Table 7, left) are computed over 5 unfinished all-zero repetitions, and the code trains every stage on the final graph, so this setting is not the one described. "Consistently" rests on one evolution model.

issues.quote: this methodology requires no additional experimentation cost and can be deployed as a plug-and-play improvement for GATE estimation under network interference.
issues.why: The practical claim has no deployment evidence, and Equation (18) concedes that under a traffic cap substantial bias remains, so "plug-and-play" only holds partly.

presentation.why: Figure 1 axis labels, tick labels and legends are printed in a font too small to read at 100% zoom.
Figure 2 histograms have unreadable axis labels and ticks; the reader depends on the caption for the variances.
Figure 3 (the main MSE figure) packs 10 panels into one text width with tiny axis text, so the values cannot be read from the figure.
Tables 3-9 and 14 are \scriptsize and then shrunk by \resizebox, so the printed numbers are very small.
The square-root paragraph breaks off mid-sentence ("..., while") and never discusses the non-monotone, positive-bias results of Table 6 (right).
"treatment proportion $t=50\%$" reuses t (the stage-count symbol) for a proportion.
No figure gives an overview of the ramp-up merging pipeline; Figure 1 is a results plot.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: To distinguish the effect of exposure variation from that of training-set size, we merge repeated experiments at a fixed treatment proportion.
paper_mismatches.why: The repeated-experiment notebooks set ramps=[0.5]*5 with one shared rollout_index, so every "repeat" treats the identical set of units and only the outcome noise is redrawn. This is duplicated data, not independent repeated experiments (the delivery's docs/migration.md line 17 says the same), so the control does not separate sample size from proportion diversity as claimed.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: we take the initial network topology $\mathcal{G}$ as baseline and repeat such evolution 5 times to generate evolved graphs with the same node set.
paper_mismatches.why: Outcomes for each stage are generated on that stage's graph, but the training loop calls model(dgl_G, ...) with dgl_G left at the last assigned (final) graph, so every stage is trained and evaluated on the final topology. The dynamic-graph results (Table 7) and their explanation do not test training on evolving graphs.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Appendix~\ref{app:exp_supp} also compares Bernoulli and complete randomization under both staggered rollout and temporally independent experiments, with similar performance across these alternatives.
paper_mismatches.why: In the "temporal independence" notebooks the uniform index is redrawn once per merge group and shared by all stages within the group, so merged stages are still nested (staggered). The left halves of Tables 8-9 therefore do not test temporally independent experiments, which explains why they match the staggered results.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: The second combines each $c_t$ with an initial stage that treats exactly one unit or cluster, approximating a zero-treatment baseline.
paper_mismatches.why: For linear-in-means the initial stage uses rollout_index < quantile(rollout_index, 0), which treats zero units (exact global control). The 2-hop notebooks use <= and treat one unit, so the "initial stage" differs across tables.
The 2-hop model uses r1=1, r2=0.5 (true GATE 2.489), but the paper gives only (beta0,beta1,r,sigma_e)=(1,1,1,0.1) and never states r2.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Bias and standard deviation (Std) are estimated from 100 Monte Carlo repetitions.
paper_mismatches.why: The notebooks run repeat_num = 1000 repetitions, and the tables are computed from all 1000 rows.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: The detailed results are reported in Table~\ref{table:lr}.
paper_mismatches.why: No delivered code or result file produces Table 10 (linear regression), Table 2 (2-hop repeated experiments), Tables 11-13 (Lagrange, MII, Hajek), Table 14 (MIT8; the MIT8 graph is absent), the Figure 2 exposure variances, or any figure. incre_2hop notebooks need a missing A_2hop.pkl.

evaluation_errors.why: Result/Dynamic_CR_unit.pkl has five unfinished repetitions (rows 995-999) left as preallocated zeros, and the summary averages over all rows. Table 7 (left, unit) therefore reports Std 0.095-0.149 and MSE 0.453/0.040/0.030/0.023/0.024. Over the 995 completed rows these are Std 0.013-0.055 and MSE 0.435/0.020/0.010/0.003/0.004, so the numbers change but no main claim reverses.

GNN features and targets are built by iterating g.nodes in NetworkX edge-insertion order (23, 1, 63, ...), while the graph passed to the GNN comes from dgl.from_networkx(g) (line 114). The delivery's own migration notes (docs/migration.md line 12) say this may relabel nodes in sorted order, so rows of the features need not match the DGL nodes. If so, message passing aggregates the wrong neighbours. The single-stage GNN biases (-0.951 unit, -0.561 cluster) are close to the graph-agnostic LR (-1.000, -0.595), which fits this. The size of the effect cannot be checked without a rerun.

problems.why: The README states that the refactored runner does not reproduce the published tables (corrected alignment, RNG streams, 197 vs 192 clusters). The tables come from legacy notebooks with unpinned torch/DGL/networkx versions.
There is no code for Tables 2 (2-hop), 10-14, Figures 1-3 or the exposure variances. The MIT8 graph is absent, and incre_2hop notebooks need a missing A_2hop.pkl.
table_output.py needs hand-edited result paths and a hand-set true GATE (2 or 2.489), and it summarises preallocated zero rows.

Ber_unit_no_ramp_final.ipynb saves to Result/NoRamp_CR_unit_res10_final.pkl, while CR_unit_no_ramp_final.ipynb saves NoRamp_CR_unit_res10_final.pkl outside Result/. Which run produced the Table 8/9 left-unit columns is therefore unclear.
The 2-hop notebooks carry a comment that the run was interrupted at seed 151 and resumed. Dynamic_CR_unit stopped at seed 995 with zero rows retained.
